questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain selected government-type terms while distinguishing a title from evidence about actual governing power.
questions.prompt: In a fictional country, a small privileged circle controls all final public decisions and prevents the wider population from sharing that power. Explain why the lesson’s term “oligarchy” fits better than simply calling this an ordinary small working committee.
questions.answer: Oligarchy concerns governing power concentrated in a few privileged people. An ordinary working committee can have a limited delegated task; being small alone does not show that it controls the country.
questions.explanation: The fictional description supplies the controlling power; no actual government is classified or judged.

markingGuide.description: Connects oligarchy to concentrated governing power among a privileged few.
Distinguishes that power from the mere size of a limited-task committee.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain selected government-type terms while distinguishing a title from evidence about actual governing power.
questions.prompt: A class index lists Oba, Emir and Obi under “traditional leadership titles”. What broad idea do these titles illustrate in this lesson, and why should a learner ask about the particular place and role before claiming that any holder has a specific legal power?
questions.answer: They illustrate leadership associated with community traditions. The title alone does not establish every holder’s functions or legal powers; these need to be checked for the particular place and role.
questions.explanation: The source supplies title examples. Their holders, jurisdiction, selection, powers and status are not treated as identical or universally outside constitutional arrangements.

markingGuide.description: Identifies leadership associated with community traditions.
Explains why a title alone does not establish a specific power.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Compare selected features of governmental arrangements without assuming that monarchy, tradition and constitutional limits are mutually exclusive.
questions.prompt: A fictional fact card says: “A king is Head of State. An elected parliament makes laws under constitutional rules.” A pupil files the card only under monarchy and crosses out constitutional government. Correct the filing, and identify one claim about the king’s tenure that the card does not establish.
questions.answer: Both labels can fit different features: monarchy describes the king as Head of State, while constitutional rules describe how authority is organised or limited. The card does not establish, for example, that the king must remain in office until death or can never leave it.
questions.explanation: The task assesses multiple classification axes and a limit of supplied evidence, not the earlier bank’s single coexistence MCQ. Source no-end-to-tenure wording is not adopted as a universal rule.

markingGuide.description: Connects monarchy to the stated Head of State.
Explains why constitutional rules can also apply.
Identifies a tenure claim not established by the card.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Compare selected features of governmental arrangements without assuming that monarchy, tradition and constitutional limits are mutually exclusive.
questions.prompt: Two fictional role cards describe how authority is recognised. One refers to a community’s customary selection of a traditional leader; the other refers to offices and powers defined by constitutional rules. Explain the different emphasis of the cards without claiming that tradition and constitutional law can never operate together.
questions.answer: The first emphasises customary selection or recognition. The second emphasises rules defining public offices and powers. These are different descriptions of authority and need not be mutually exclusive in every arrangement.
questions.explanation: The supplied cases are illustrative. No specific Nigerian traditional institution’s legal status is decided.

markingGuide.description: Identifies custom/recognition as the first emphasis.
Identifies constitutionally defined offices/powers as the second.
Avoids treating the two descriptions as necessarily incompatible.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain a party system as a pattern of party competition and relationships, distinguishing it from one party’s name or policies.
questions.prompt: A report describes how several political parties compete for support and cooperate or oppose one another. A separate leaflet describes the policies of just one party. Explain which document is more directly about a party system and why.
questions.answer: The report is about a party system because it describes a pattern of relationships and competition among parties. A single party’s policy leaflet describes that organisation’s ideas, rather than the whole pattern.
questions.explanation: This is a conceptual comparison using fictional documents, not a current-country classification.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the report’s inter-party pattern.
Distinguishes that pattern from one party’s policies.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain a party system as a pattern of party competition and relationships, distinguishing it from one party’s name or policies.
questions.prompt: A learner knows the name and colour of one fictional political party and claims to know the country’s party system. Identify two further kinds of information that would be useful before making such a claim.
questions.answer: It would help to know which other parties can compete and how support or effective competition is distributed among them. A name and colour alone do not show these relationships.
questions.explanation: Accept other relevant information about inter-party relationships. Neither a logo nor a raw party count alone settles every typology.

markingGuide.description: Identifies information about other parties’ ability to compete.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Compare selected one-party, two-party and multiparty patterns, distinguishing legal permission, electoral dominance and coalition cooperation.
questions.prompt: Compare these fictional cases: in one, rules permit only one party to contest for governing power; in the other, several parties may compete but the same party has won repeatedly. Why does repeated victory alone not prove that both cases have the same restriction?
questions.answer: The first explicitly restricts competition to one party. The second states an electoral outcome, not a ban on other parties. Repeated wins do not by themselves prove that rivals are forbidden to compete.
questions.explanation: A narrow one-party restriction example is used; no real country label or all one-party/dominant-party variants are claimed.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the explicit restriction in the first case.
Distinguishes repeated victory from evidence of a ban.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Compare selected one-party, two-party and multiparty patterns, distinguishing legal permission, electoral dominance and coalition cooperation.
questions.prompt: In a fictional system, two major parties usually dominate elections, but smaller parties also contest seats. A pupil says the smaller parties must be breaking the meaning of “two-party system”. Explain the mistake.
questions.answer: The term can describe dominance by two major parties rather than a rule allowing exactly two parties to exist. Smaller parties can therefore compete without contradicting that description.
questions.explanation: PEO explicitly distinguishes dominance from a strict two-party count and qualifies its own Australian example; no Australian or Nigerian seat totals are assessed.

markingGuide.description: Explains dominance rather than an exact legal limit.
Applies that distinction to the smaller parties in the case.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Compare selected one-party, two-party and multiparty patterns, distinguishing legal permission, electoral dominance and coalition cooperation.
questions.prompt: A fictional country has several parties with a realistic chance to gain governing power, either separately or by cooperating. Why can this fit a multiparty pattern, and why does the description not guarantee that every government must be a coalition?
questions.answer: More than two parties can compete effectively for governing power. They may cooperate, but a party could also obtain enough support on its own; the description gives possibilities rather than an inevitable coalition.
questions.explanation: This narrow fictional pattern does not promise stability or instability, prescribe a majority rule for Nigeria or adopt the handout’s historical country examples.

markingGuide.description: Explains effective competition involving several parties.
Distinguishes possible cooperation from an unavoidable coalition.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Compare selected one-party, two-party and multiparty patterns, distinguishing legal permission, electoral dominance and coalition cooperation.
questions.prompt: Two fictional parties cooperate to form a governing coalition but keep separate names, policies and meetings. Someone calls the coalition a new one-party system merely because there is one government. Explain why that conclusion does not follow.
questions.answer: One government can be supported by more than one party. Cooperating in a coalition does not by itself merge the parties or ban other parties from competing.
questions.explanation: PEO’s coalition-identity explanation supports the conceptual point; no full country-specific government-formation rule is applied.

markingGuide.description: Distinguishes the number of governments from the number of cooperating parties.
Explains that coalition cooperation does not itself erase separate party identities or establish a ban.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish party and pressure-group purposes when membership or campaign methods overlap, without inferring legal registration from a fictional description.
questions.prompt: A fictional political party and a fictional pressure group both publish posters about the same public issue. A pupil says the shared method proves they are the same kind of organisation. Explain why the method is insufficient and what purpose should also be checked.
questions.answer: Posters are a method that different organisations can use. Check whether the organisation seeks representatives in government through elections, chiefly seeks to influence decisions on an issue, or has a more complex combination of activities.
questions.explanation: This tests an evidence boundary and overlapping methods, rather than repeating the earlier bank’s direct party-versus-group definition question.

markingGuide.description: Explains that a shared method does not establish organisational identity.
Identifies the need to check purposes beyond the method.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish party and pressure-group purposes when membership or campaign methods overlap, without inferring legal registration from a fictional description.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain selected policy-development, scrutiny and information functions of political parties and pressure groups using supplied fictional cases.
questions.prompt: Members of a fictional party collect different suggestions, debate them and agree a policy proposal to present to voters. Explain the function shown and how agreeing a proposal differs from proving that every voter supports it.
questions.answer: The party is developing and organising policy choices. Agreement within the party establishes its proposal, not the views of every voter, who may compare it with alternatives.
questions.explanation: This adds a policy-making and inference task rather than another generic election-definition item. No proposal is supplied for pupils to advocate.

markingGuide.description: Explains policy development/organisation of choices.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.topic: Peer behaviours that influence decision Making
questions.learningObjective: Explain peer pressure as influence from peers on choices, including expectations about fitting in.
questions.prompt: A fictional pupil wants to follow an agreed classroom plan but changes the decision after classmates say that joining them is the only way to fit in. Explain the peer-pressure element in this situation.
questions.answer: The classmates’ expectation about belonging influences the pupil’s choice. The decision changes to gain acceptance rather than simply because the pupil independently prefers the other plan.
questions.explanation: No learner’s own experience is requested; the example explains a concept rather than diagnosing a pupil.

markingGuide.description: Identifies influence from peers or their expectation.
Connects fitting in/acceptance with the changed decision.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.topic: Peer behaviours that influence decision Making
questions.learningObjective: Demonstrate and distinguish selected positive and negative peer-influence examples in an actually observed, bounded fictional role.
questions.prompt: In an actual supervised role with an adult playing a fictional peer, demonstrate two short examples about a harmless classroom turn-taking game. First invite the partner to respect agreed turns. Then use the supplied pretend line “Let us skip the agreed turn” as an example of unhelpful influence. Immediately step out of role and explain the difference. Do not actually skip anyone’s turn or pressure another pupil.
questions.answer: Observed evidence: a constructive invitation about agreed turns, the bounded pretend unhelpful line and an out-of-role explanation that one supports fairness while the other invites breaking the agreement.
questions.explanation: Use an adult partner, fictional roles and a stop option. This is representation and explanation, not an assignment to manipulate a real peer. No performance occurred during authoring.

markingGuide.description: Actually gives a constructive invitation respecting agreed turns.
Performs only the supplied harmless pretend line, without carrying out exclusion.
Steps out of role and clearly distinguishes the two influences.
